---
title: "Backtracking: Choose, Explore, Undo"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning for algorithm interviews, with a worked example and proof."
---

## When to recognise this technique

When the problem asks for all valid subsets, paths, permutations or assignments.

## Start with the question

**What mathematical condition allows pruning before exploring a whole branch?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
\mathcal S(x)=\bigcup_{a\in A(x)}\mathcal S(T(x,a))
$$

**Every symbol explained:** x is the current partial solution/state; A(x) is the set of allowed next choices; T(x,a) is the state after choice a; S(x) is the family of complete valid solutions reachable from x; union combines solutions from all legal children.

**Substitute actual values:** For permutations of [1,2], initial choices are 1 or 2. Choosing 1 leaves [2] giving [1,2]; choosing 2 leaves [1] giving [2,1]. The union contains two solutions.

## Why the mathematics works

Enumerating every valid next choice ensures completeness; rejecting a partial state is safe only when no completion could satisfy the constraints. An implementation may mutate a shared path, recurse and undo to restore the previous state.

## Limits and counterexamples

Not all DFS is backtracking: reachability DFS need not restore a path for alternative assignments. Conversely, backtracking may explore a tree of choices rather than the original input graph.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: state + choices + validity condition + base case + undo. Every prune requires an impossibility argument.**

Try explaining the formula aloud using the numerical example, then reproduce the proof from memory. An interview answer must justify the relationship, not just quote it.

**Practice problems:** Permutations; N-Queens.
